Business quality

ROCE Return on Capital Employed

How much profit a business earns on every rupee put into it.

Example. A shop uses ₹10 lakh of capital and earns ₹2 lakh operating profit in a year. ROCE is 20%. A second shop needs ₹50 lakh to earn the same ₹2 lakh, a ROCE of 4%. Same profit, but the first business is five times better at turning money into money.

Why it matters. This is the single best test of business quality. High ROCE sustained over years is what makes a stock compound. Above 18% is strong in India; below 8% means the business barely beats a fixed deposit.

ROE Return on Equity

Profit earned on the shareholders' own money.

Example. A company has ₹100 crore of shareholder equity and makes ₹18 crore net profit. ROE is 18%: the owners' money grew 18% that year.

Why it matters. Similar to ROCE but ignores debt. That's the trap: a company can show a wonderful ROE simply by borrowing heavily. Always read ROE next to debt-to-equity, never alone.

Gross margin

What's left from each rupee of sales after the direct cost of making the product.

Example. Sell a shirt for ₹1,000; cloth and stitching cost ₹600. Gross margin is 40%.

Why it matters. High margins usually mean a brand people pay extra for, or a genuine cost advantage. Rising margins mean pricing power is improving. Falling margins are one of the earliest warning signs a business is losing its edge.

Operating cash flow

Actual cash the business collected from operations, not accounting profit.

Example. A company reports ₹100 crore profit but collected only ₹40 crore in cash, because ₹60 crore is still owed by customers. Profit says one thing; cash says another.

Why it matters. Profit is an opinion, cash is a fact. Profit can be shaped by accounting choices; cash in the bank cannot. When cash flow consistently exceeds reported profit, earnings quality is high.

Debt & safety

Debt to Equity

How much the company has borrowed compared with the owners' own money.

Example. ₹30 crore of loans against ₹100 crore of shareholder equity gives a ratio of 0.3.

Why it matters. Debt magnifies both directions. In a good year it boosts returns; in a bad year it can end the company. Below 0.3 is comfortable, above 1.5 means lenders have more at stake than owners.

Current ratio

Whether the company can pay bills due within a year using assets it can convert within a year.

Example. ₹60 crore in current assets against ₹30 crore of current liabilities gives a ratio of 2.

Why it matters. Below 1 means short-term obligations exceed short-term resources, which forces borrowing at bad moments. A rising ratio year on year means liquidity is improving.

Promoter pledging

Promoters using their own shares as collateral for personal loans.

Example. A promoter holds 50% of the company and has pledged 30% of that stake to a lender.

Why it matters. One of the loudest red flags in Indian markets. If the price falls, lenders can sell the pledged shares, which pushes the price down further, a spiral that has destroyed several listed companies.

Valuation

P/E ratio Price to Earnings

How many years of current profit you're paying for the shares.

Example. A share costs ₹500 and earns ₹25 per share a year. P/E is 20, meaning you pay twenty years of current earnings.

Why it matters. A rough but honest first check. High P/E means the market expects growth; if that growth fails to arrive, the price falls hard. Comparing P/E is only meaningful within the same industry. An IT company and a bank are not comparable.

Market capitalisation

What the entire company costs at today's price.

Example. 10 crore shares at ₹500 each means a market cap of ₹5,000 crore.

Why it matters. This, not the share price, tells you the size of the company. A ₹50 share is not 'cheap' and a ₹5,000 share is not 'expensive'. The share price alone tells you nothing without the share count.

EPS Earnings Per Share

Profit divided by the number of shares.

Example. ₹250 crore profit across 10 crore shares gives EPS of ₹25.

Why it matters. Watch it across years rather than in isolation. Rising EPS is good, unless it rose because the company bought back shares rather than because profit actually grew.

Scores

Piotroski F-Score

Nine pass-or-fail tests of financial health, scored out of 9.

Example. A company that is profitable, generates cash, is reducing debt and improving margins might score 8 or 9. One that is losing money with rising debt scores 1 or 2.

Why it matters. Created by accounting professor Joseph Piotroski in 2000. His research found that among cheap-looking stocks, the high scorers substantially outperformed the low scorers. It separates genuine bargains from businesses that are cheap for good reason.

Mohanram G-Score

A companion test for growth companies, checking whether the growth is durable.

Example. A fast-growing company generating strong cash, investing in capacity and holding its margins scores well. One growing on borrowed money with weak cash scores poorly.

Why it matters. Piotroski's test suits cheap stocks; Mohanram's suits expensive ones. Altaha uses an adapted version, because the original needs research-spending data that Indian filings don't reliably publish, which is why our version is labelled 'adapted' and every threshold is disclosed.

Price & trend

Moving average

The average closing price over a set number of days, redrawn each day.

Example. The 50-day moving average is the average of the last 50 closes. Tomorrow it drops the oldest day and adds the newest.

Why it matters. It strips out daily noise so the underlying direction is visible. When price sits above a rising average, and short averages sit above long ones, that's the textbook definition of an uptrend.

RSI Relative Strength Index

A 0 to 100 gauge of how hard a stock has been bought or sold recently.

Example. RSI of 75 means buying has been intense for several weeks. RSI of 25 means heavy selling.

Why it matters. Above roughly 70 the move is often stretched and due a pause; below 30 it may be oversold. But a strong stock can stay 'overbought' for months. RSI describes intensity, it does not predict reversal.

MACD

Compares a fast and a slow moving average to show whether momentum is building or fading.

Example. When the fast line crosses above the slow line and the gap widens, momentum is accelerating.

Why it matters. It answers a different question from 'is the price up'. It asks whether the move is gaining strength or running out of steam.

ADX Average Directional Index

Measures how strongly a stock is trending, in either direction.

Example. ADX of 35 means a powerful trend. ADX of 12 means price is drifting sideways with no conviction.

Why it matters. It says nothing about up or down, only about strength. Below 20 most trend signals become unreliable, because there is no trend to follow.

Bollinger Bands

A channel drawn two standard deviations either side of a 20-day average.

Example. Price near the upper band is at the strong end of its recent range; near the lower band, the weak end.

Why it matters. When the bands narrow sharply, volatility has compressed and a large move often follows, though the squeeze tells you a move is coming, not which way.

Supertrend

A line that sits below price in an uptrend and above it in a downtrend, adjusting for volatility.

Example. Price closing above the line is a bullish regime; closing below flips it bearish.

Why it matters. A simple, unambiguous regime filter. Its value is that it gives a clear line rather than a judgement call, useful precisely because it removes discretion.

Volume

Volume

The number of shares that changed hands.

Example. A stock rising 5% on triple its usual volume is a very different event from rising 5% on half its usual volume.

Why it matters. Volume is the conviction behind a price move. Price tells you what happened; volume tells you how many people meant it.

Accumulation & distribution

Whether more shares trade on rising days or on falling days.

Example. Over twenty sessions, if up-day volume is 1.8 times down-day volume, buyers have been more aggressive than sellers.

Why it matters. Large investors cannot hide their footprint. Sustained accumulation often appears in volume before it shows up in price.

OBV On-Balance Volume

A running total that adds volume on up days and subtracts it on down days.

Example. If price makes a new high but OBV doesn't, fewer shares are supporting each rise. The move is hollow.

Why it matters. That divergence between price and OBV is one of the more reliable early warnings that a rally is losing its base.

Ownership

FII and DII

Foreign and domestic institutional investors, the large professional funds.

Example. FIIs are overseas funds; DIIs are Indian mutual funds, insurers and pension funds.

Why it matters. They move markets by size alone, and they research before buying. A meaningful institutional stake means the company has passed outside scrutiny, though institutions are wrong regularly, and the data is quarterly, so it lags.

Promoter holding

The stake held by the founding family or parent group.

Example. Promoters holding 55% means more than half the company is owned by the people running it.

Why it matters. High and stable promoter holding means their wealth rises and falls with yours. A stake falling across consecutive quarters deserves attention: the people who know the business best are stepping back.

Shareholding pattern

The quarterly filing showing exactly who owns the company.

Example. Promoters 55%, institutions 27%, public 18%, filed with the exchanges every quarter.

Why it matters. It's the only regular window into who is buying and selling in size. Because it's quarterly, it can be up to three months old, so it is useful for direction, not for timing.
